title: La Chiesa Madre
description:
La Chiesa Madre 1999


Based on a photograph I took in Positano in 1999, this piece began with a compositional idea, using a telephoto lens to flatten the perspective, emphasising the cascading geometry typical of the town’s architecture. I painted the image in grayscale acrylic on board to heighten its accented sunset reflections.

This piece works especially well as a Giclée Hahnemühle Photorag print. It’s a more expensive paper, but worth it — the image truly comes to life on its surface. The super-matte finish enhances muted blacks, preserves fine detail, and offers even colour reproduction. Its subtle texture and smooth, cotton feel create beautifully soft colour gradients.


The original has been sold, but replica prints on canvas are available in three sizes, framed or unframed.

title: Flow 98
description:
Accidental Aesthetics I
1991– by [Your Name]

This work is part of a series of accidental aesthetics, where natural or unexpected patterns serve as the starting point for abstract compositions. In this piece, the textures were inspired by the way cheese expands under foil during cooking. As the foil is peeled away, it reveals intricate surface patterns—formed through heat and pressure—that echo the shapes we see across nature.

The idea behind the work is simple: physical reactions create forms, and those forms often repeat themselves. Whether it’s melted cheese, the surface of a planet, or the structure of a cell, these visual patterns connect the smallest moments to the largest scales of the universe.

title: Binomial
description:
Binomial, 1984

As a teenager in the 1960s, I was fascinated by geometric art and often created my own patterns and structures. When I later discovered the work of Victor Vasarely and M. C. Escher, I realised that everything I was exploring had already been done brilliantly and completely. That realisation stopped me from pursuing it further as a visual art form.

Instead, I began incorporating those ideas into my photography. This image is part of that evolution. It’s a projection of one of Escher’s works onto the human body. The photograph plays with light, void, and form, asking the viewer’s brain to complete what’s left out. After many experiments in the 1970s, I finally captured the image as I imagined it in 1984.

title: Venus
description:
Venus, 1978

This piece is part of my 'Still in Motion' photography series, where I combined long exposure with deliberate camera movement—what I often think of as “painting with the camera.” The original photograph was taken in 1978 as part of an exploration into motion and body form through analog means.

Years later, with the introduction of digital editing, I returned to the image, not to enhance it, but to reduce it. I stripped away much of the colour and detail, minimising the image to just what was needed for recognition. What remains is a light, nearly abstract impression that still conveys movement and presence, while allowing the viewer’s imagination to fill in the rest.

title: Persepolis
description:
Persepolis 2005


This photograph was taken just outside the ruins of Persepolis in southern Iran. Behind me stood two-and-a-half-thousand years of history, and in front of me—a newly built car park with young trees. While everyone else pointed their cameras toward the ruins, I looked slightly ridiculous pointing mine the other way. After all, the ruins have been photographed millions of times, but I think this picture is unique.

Shot on film, this is a fully analog image with no digital manipulation. Everything you see was created in-camera through exposure, depth of field, and film speed.

This piece works especially well as a Giclée Hahnemühle Photo Rag print. It’s a more expensive paper, but worth it — the image truly comes to life on its surface. The super-matte finish enhances muted blacks, preserves fine detail, and offers even colour reproduction. Its subtle texture and smooth, cotton feel create beautifully soft colour gradients.

title: Bipolarity
description:
Bipolarity, 2000

This piece began in early 2000 and was completed later that same year—intentionally finished within the calendar year to mark the new millennium. It was worked on in short, scattered sessions over about ten months, fitting into the natural interruptions of everyday life.

The painting reflects the bipolar nature of the world around us: north-south, east-west, rich-poor, black-white, have-have-not. For me, both sides are equally valuable, different but balanced. There’s no hierarchy. At its heart, though, the aim was simple: to create bold, colourful graphics that bring life to a wall.

title: Salvador
description:
Dalí, 2002

If I had to name the artists who most impressed me as a young boy, three come to mind; Dalí and Picasso as painters, and Gaudí as an architect. This is the Dalí portrait. There’s also a matching one of Picasso.

It took me years to figure out how to pay tribute to them visually. I didn’t want to simply paint a portrait, I was waiting for the right idea. This concept finally came together in 2002. As for Gaudí, I still haven’t found the right approach, and I’m not sure if I ever will.

These are large acrylic paintings on canvas and are available as originals, as well as replica prints on canvas (framed or unframed).

title: You
description:
You 2003


Although most of my work is driven by graphic composition, every now and then something compels me to manifest an idea more directly. This piece represents how I imagine life: intersecting dimensions, each its own universe. Where they all overlap is the life of the individual. That point of convergence is the viewer, in that moment. Even while viewing the painting, all dimensions are active, creating a one-time connection between the image and the person standing in front of it.

This is a large acrylic on canvas. Due to the sculptural texture at its center, it cannot be faithfully reproduced and is only available as an original.
